title: Decorating Views
text:
A view in this package has one job: decide what to show. It looks at the request, talks to whatever data it needs, and returns a dict. It never touches HTML. The template does the showing, and the decorator is the handshake between them.
That split is the point. Views stay small and testable, templates stay editable by someone who never opens a Python file, and FastAPI keeps doing all the things it is good at underneath.

Decorator order
The route decorator goes on the outside. @fastapi_chameleon.template(...) sits directly on the function.
@router.post('/')
@fastapi_chameleon.template('home/index.pt')
async def home_post(request: fastapi.Request):
    form = await request.form()
    vm = PersonViewModel(**form)
    return vm.model_dump()
FastAPI’s dependency injection does not notice the decorator is there. Path parameters, query parameters, Request, and Depends(...) all resolve exactly as before, because the wrapper is built with functools.wraps and the decorator is typed with ParamSpec-based overloads. Your parameters still appear in the OpenAPI schema, and your type checker still sees the original signature.


Three ways to name the template
@fastapi_chameleon.template('home/index.pt')   # explicit template file
@fastapi_chameleon.template()                  # inferred template name
@fastapi_chameleon.template                    # bare form, also inferred
The explicit form is resolved relative to the folder you passed to global_init(). Nothing clever happens, which is exactly why most people use it.
The inferred forms are for the tidy-minded. Leave the name off and the decorator works it out from where the view lives:

The file is {module}/{function_name} under the template folder, where module is the last segment of the view’s dotted module name.
An .html file is preferred. If it does not exist, .pt is used.
def index() in views/home.py resolves to templates/home/index.html, falling back to templates/home/index.pt.

Inference happens once, when the module is imported, so there is no filesystem lookup per request. It also means the engine must already know its folder when the view module is imported. If global_init() has not run yet, the folder silently defaults to templates relative to the current working directory, and a later global_init() does not go back and re-resolve names that were already derived. Explicit template names never have this problem. Pick inference when your project layout is disciplined, and pick explicit names when you would rather read the path than remember the rule.


What a view may return
Three outcomes, and only three.







Return value
Result




dict
Rendered through the template as its variables.


any fastapi.Response
Passed through untouched. The template is skipped.


anything else (None, a Pydantic model, a list)
FastAPIChameleonException is raised at request time.



The second row is how Shelf Life’s login form works. A successful login should not render the login page again, it should send the customer to their account. Returning a Response says “I have already decided what to send, step aside”:
@router.post('/account/login')
@fastapi_chameleon.template('account/login.pt')
async def login(request: fastapi.Request):
    user = await try_login(request)
    if user:
        return fastapi.responses.RedirectResponse('/account', status_code=302)

    return {'error': 'Invalid login'}  # re-render the form with an error
The third row is strict on purpose. A view that returns None because someone forgot the return statement, or returns a Pydantic model straight from the database layer, fails loudly with Invalid return type <class 'NoneType'> rather than rendering a blank page at 2am. Convert first: model.model_dump() for Pydantic, dataclasses.asdict(obj) for dataclasses, {'books': books} for a list.


Non-HTML output
Templates are not only for pages. Shelf Life’s sitemap is a Chameleon template too, and the decorator takes a mimetype for exactly that:
@router.get('/sitemap.xml')
@fastapi_chameleon.template('seo/sitemap.pt', mimetype='application/xml')
def sitemap():
    return {'urls': load_urls()}
A rendered dict always goes out with status 200. Error pages raised with not_found() or generic_error() ignore this mimetype and are always text/html, because a browser that asked for a sitemap and got a 404 should still see a readable page. See Friendly Error Pages.


Manual rendering with response()
Sometimes you want the wheel. A status code other than 200, a view that renders one of several different templates depending on the data, a response assembled outside a route entirely. For those, skip the decorator and call response():
@router.get('/report')
def report():
    return fastapi_chameleon.response('reports/summary.pt', status_code=202, title='Monthly summary')
It renders the template with the keyword arguments as the model and returns a fastapi.Response with the given mimetype (default text/html) and status_code (default 200). It needs global_init() to have run, like everything else in the package.
And when you want the HTML as a plain string, say for the body of a confirmation email or an assertion in a test, use fastapi_chameleon.engine.render(template_file, **model).


Reference

template()
response()

title: Testing and CI
text:
Here is the pleasant secret of this package: a decorated view is still just a Python function. No server, no port, no TestClient, no fixture that spins up an app. You call the view, you get back a fastapi.Response, and you look inside it. This is how the package tests itself, and it is how Shelf Life’s test suite runs in well under a second.

A fixture for the engine
The engine is module-global, one per process, so tests need two things from a fixture: initialise it before the test, and clear it afterwards so the next test starts clean.
# conftest.py
from pathlib import Path

import pytest

import fastapi_chameleon as fc


@pytest.fixture
def setup_global_template(pytestconfig):
    fc.global_init(Path(pytestconfig.rootdir, 'tests', 'templates'))
    yield
    fc.engine.clear()  # do not leak engine state between tests
Two details keep this reliable:

global_init() ignores repeat calls by default. If a test calls it directly with a different folder, pass cache_init=False.
Always clear in teardown. A test that asserts “rendering before global_init() raises” will pass or fail depending on which test ran before it otherwise, and flaky tests that depend on ordering are the kind you only notice in CI on a Friday.



Calling views directly
# test_views.py
import asyncio

import fastapi

import fastapi_chameleon as fc


def test_index_renders(setup_global_template):
    @fc.template('home/index.pt')
    def index(name: str):
        return {'name': name}

    resp = index('Sam')
    assert isinstance(resp, fastapi.Response)
    assert resp.status_code == 200
    assert resp.media_type == 'text/html'
    assert 'Sam' in resp.body.decode('utf-8')


def test_async_index_renders(setup_global_template):
    @fc.template('home/index.pt')
    async def index(name: str):
        return {'name': name}

    resp = asyncio.run(index('Sam'))
    assert resp.status_code == 200


def test_missing_item_gives_404(setup_global_template):
    @fc.template('home/index.pt')
    def item(item_id: int):
        fc.not_found()

    resp = item(42)
    assert resp.status_code == 404
Pass view arguments positionally or by keyword, exactly as FastAPI would. Async views are one asyncio.run() away. If a view takes a Request, build one with fastapi.Request(scope) or use TestClient for that particular test.


Through FastAPI
When the thing under test is the routing, the dependencies, or the middleware rather than the view, use FastAPI’s TestClient against the real app. Decorated views need nothing special:
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient

from my_app.main import app


def test_home_page():
    client = TestClient(app)
    resp = client.get('/')
    assert resp.status_code == 200
    assert resp.headers['content-type'].startswith('text/html')
Make sure global_init() runs when my_app.main is imported, or call it in a session fixture before the app is created.


CI
The package has no compiled parts and two dependencies, so CI is a pytest run per interpreter and nothing more. A GitHub Actions matrix:
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      matrix:
        python-version: ['3.10', '3.11', '3.12', '3.13', '3.14']
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@v5
      - run: uv run --python ${{ matrix.python-version }} --with pytest --with-editable . pytest
Locally, tox with the tox.ini in the repository does the same thing across whichever interpreters you have installed.

title: How It Works
text:
The whole library is three short modules, and you can read engine.py in the time it takes to make coffee. But the behaviour that matters is about timing: what happens once when your app imports, what happens on every request, and how an error page gets from a function three layers deep back up to the browser. Know those three and every rule in the rest of this guide becomes obvious.

Act one: the engine
global_init() stores two module-level values in fastapi_chameleon.engine: a Chameleon PageTemplateLoader and the template folder path. That is the entire state of the library. Every render in the process goes through that one loader, which is why global_init() is called once, why a second call is ignored by default, and why tests clear it between runs with engine.clear().
Think of it as the shop’s single key cabinet. Everyone who needs a template goes to the same cabinet, and you set up the cabinet before opening the doors.


Act two: decoration time
@template(...) runs when the view module is imported, not when a request arrives. At that moment it makes three decisions and never revisits them:

Which template. An explicit name is kept as-is. A missing name is derived from the view’s module and function name, and the .html or .pt choice is made by checking the filesystem once.
Sync or async. inspect.iscoroutinefunction picks a synchronous or asynchronous wrapper. The async wrapper awaits the view, the sync one calls it, and both then render.
The signature. The wrapper is wrapped with functools.wraps, and template() is typed with ParamSpec-based overloads, so FastAPI’s dependency injection and your type checker both see the original parameters, not *args, **kwargs.

Because the template folder is read at decoration time for name inference, global_init() has to run before the view module is imported. If it has not, the folder defaults to templates relative to the current working directory. This is the single most important timing rule in the package, and it only bites the inferred-name forms.


Act three: request time
A request comes in. FastAPI resolves the dependencies and calls the wrapper, which calls the view and looks at what came back:

A fastapi.Response is returned as-is. The template is never touched.
A dict is handed to the loader as the template model, and the HTML comes back in a fastapi.Response with the decorator’s mimetype and status 200.
Anything else raises FastAPIChameleonException.

Rendering before global_init() has run raises FastAPIChameleonException too. A template file that does not exist raises ValueError from Chameleon’s loader.


The emergency exits
not_found() and generic_error() do not return. They raise FastAPIChameleonNotFoundException or FastAPIChameleonGenericException, both subclasses of FastAPIChameleonException. The wrapper from act two has a try around the view call that catches exactly those two types, and nothing else. When it catches one, it renders the exception’s template with the exception’s status, always as text/html. Any other exception passes straight through to FastAPI.
That is why the functions work from anywhere below a decorated view: exceptions travel up the call stack for free, so a repository can refuse a request and the decorator at the top turns the refusal into a page. It is also why they do nothing useful outside one. No wrapper, no try, no page.


Template caching
Chameleon compiles each template to a Python module on first use and keeps it in memory. With auto_reload=False, that compiled version serves every request for the rest of the process. With auto_reload=True, the loader checks the file’s modification time before each use and recompiles when it changed. The first request after a deploy pays the compile cost; every request after that is a function call.


Source
The code is short and readable, and reading it is the fastest way to confirm anything on this page: engine.py and exceptions.py.

title: FAQ
text:
The questions that come up once the shop is open and real customers are clicking things.

Can I use Jinja instead of Chameleon?
Not with this package, but you do not have to choose blind. fastapi-jinja is the sister project with the same shape: one global_init(), one @template decorator, views that return dicts. Swapping between them is mostly a matter of which attribute syntax you prefer.


Does it work with APIRouter?
Yes. Put @router.get(...) on the outside and @fastapi_chameleon.template(...) directly on the function, exactly as with @app.get(...).


Do async views work?
Yes. The decorator detects a coroutine function at decoration time and awaits it. Nothing else changes, and sync and async views can live side by side in the same router.


Can I return a Pydantic model from a view?
No. Return model.model_dump(). Only a dict or a fastapi.Response is accepted, and anything else raises FastAPIChameleonException with a message naming the type it got instead.


How do I pass the request to the template?
Put it in the dict: return {'request': request, 'title': 'Home'}. The template can then read ${request.url.path} or anything else on it. There is no magic request variable, which also means there is nothing to forget to configure.


Can I have more than one template folder?
Not at the same time. There is one loader per process. Use subfolders of a single root and refer to them in template paths, such as admin/users.pt.


Why does my 404 page come back as JSON, or as a 500?
Because not_found() was called from code that is not below a @template-decorated view. The decorator is the thing that turns the exception into a page, and without it the exception is just an exception. Decorate the route, or raise fastapi.HTTPException(404) from undecorated code. See Friendly Error Pages.


Why are my template edits not showing up?
auto_reload is False by default and templates are compiled once. Pass auto_reload=True to global_init() while developing. Note that a second global_init() call does not change the setting unless you pass cache_init=False. See Configuration.


Should I use the template name inference?
If your project is laid out as {module}/{function}.pt and global_init() runs before your view modules are imported, inference is tidy and saves a string per view. If you would rather read the path than remember the rule, name templates explicitly. Both are fully supported. See Decorating Views.


What Python versions are supported?
Python 3.10 and newer. The test suite runs on 3.10 through 3.15.


Where is the full list of errors?
Troubleshooting lists every exception the package or Chameleon raises, what it means, and how to fix it, in the order you should check things.

title: Configuration
text:
There is pleasingly little to configure. One function, three parameters, and no environment variables, settings files, or command-line flags hiding behind them. Everything the engine knows, it learned from a single global_init() call at startup.

global_init() parameters









Parameter
Type
Default
Effect




template_folder
str or os.PathLike
required
Root folder for every template path. Must exist and be a directory, otherwise FastAPIChameleonException is raised.


auto_reload
bool
False
When True, Chameleon checks template files for changes on each use and recompiles them. When False, each template is compiled once per process.


cache_init
bool
True
When True, a call made after the engine is already initialized is ignored. When False, the call replaces the loader and folder.



Every row in that table was checked against the source and then by running it. The auto_reload flag is handed straight to Chameleon’s PageTemplateLoader, so its behaviour is Chameleon’s behaviour.


Calling global_init() more than once
This is the one place people get tripped up, because the default is to politely ignore you.







Situation
Result




Second call, cache_init=True (default)
Silently ignored. The first folder and auto_reload setting stay in effect.


Second call, cache_init=False
New loader and folder take effect for every template rendered from now on.


engine.clear() then global_init()
Same as a first call.



The consequence: you cannot flip auto_reload by calling global_init() a second time with the defaults. The engine will keep whatever it was told first. Pass cache_init=False, or call fastapi_chameleon.engine.clear() and start over. This design is deliberate. It means a library or a plugin that calls global_init() defensively cannot stomp on the app’s own configuration.


Development versus production
import os
from pathlib import Path

import fastapi_chameleon

dev_mode = os.environ.get('APP_ENV', 'dev') == 'dev'  # your own switch, the package reads no env vars

BASE_DIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
fastapi_chameleon.global_init(BASE_DIR / 'templates', auto_reload=dev_mode)
With auto_reload=False, Chameleon compiles each template to Python the first time it is used and reuses that compiled version for the life of the process. Rendering a page becomes a function call, which is why Chameleon has a reputation for speed. That is the setting you want under load. With auto_reload=True, every use checks the file’s modification time first. Cheap, but not free, and pointless on a server where nobody is editing templates.


The decorator
@template(template_file=None, mimetype='text/html') has two options:








Parameter
Default
Effect




template_file
None
Template path relative to the folder. None means infer {module}/{function}.html, then .pt.


mimetype
'text/html'
Content type of the response for a rendered dict. Ignored for error pages.



There is no status_code parameter on the decorator, and that is on purpose. A rendered dict is always a 200. For another status use response(), and for error pages use generic_error(), each of which makes the status visible at the call site instead of hiding it in a decorator argument.


Where global_init() goes
Call it at import time in the module that creates the app, before the view modules are imported. When views live in their own module, the order looks like this:
# main.py
import fastapi
import fastapi_chameleon

app = fastapi.FastAPI()
fastapi_chameleon.global_init('templates')

from views import home  # noqa: E402  imported after init on purpose

app.include_router(home.router)
The order matters only for views that let the decorator infer the template name. Views with explicit template names resolve them at request time against whatever folder is configured then, so they are indifferent to import order.

title: template()
not_found()
text:
Short-circuit the current view and render a friendly 404 page.


Usage
Source


not_found(four04template_file="errors/404.pt")


Call this from inside a template()-decorated view when a resource cannot be found. It raises an exception that the decorator catches and turns into an HTTP 404 response rendered from four04template_file. This function never returns normally.
Example:
@app.get('/items/{item_id}')
@fastapi_chameleon.template('catalog/item.pt')
def item(item_id: int):
    item = repo.get(item_id)
    if not item:
        fastapi_chameleon.not_found()
    return {'item': item}


Parameters


four04template_file: str = "errors/404.pt"

The template to render for the 404 response (path relative to the template folder). Defaults to errors/404.pt.





Raises


 FastAPIChameleonNotFoundException

Always; this is how the 404 is signalled to the decorator.

title: global_init()
text:
Initialize the Chameleon template engine for your app.


Usage
Source


global_init(template_folder, auto_reload=False, cache_init=True)


Call this once at startup, pointing it at the folder that holds your *.pt templates. Template paths used elsewhere (in template(), response(), not_found(), and generic_error()) are resolved relative to this folder. Call it before the modules that define decorated views are imported, so that template name inference sees the right folder.
Example:
from pathlib import Path
import fastapi_chameleon
templates = Path(__file__).resolve().parent / 'templates'
fastapi_chameleon.global_init(templates, auto_reload=dev_mode)


Parameters


template_folder: Union[str, os.PathLike[str]]

Path to the folder containing your Chameleon templates, as a str or any os.PathLike such as pathlib.Path.

auto_reload: bool = False

Reload templates from disk when they change. Handy in development; leave False in production. Defaults to False.

cache_init: bool = True

When True (the default), a second call is a no-op once the engine is already initialized. Pass False to force re-initialization (for example, to switch template folders in tests).





Raises


 FastAPIChameleonException

If template_folder is empty or is not a directory.

title: exceptions.FastAPIChameleonNotFoundException
text:
Signals a 404 response from inside a decorated view.


Usage
Source


exceptions.FastAPIChameleonNotFoundException(
    message=None, four04template_file="errors/404.pt"
)


Raised by not_found() and caught by the template() decorator, which renders template_file with an HTTP 404 status. You normally raise it indirectly via not_found() rather than constructing it yourself.
Example:
try:
    fastapi_chameleon.not_found('errors/custom_404.pt')
except FastAPIChameleonNotFoundException as e:
    assert e.template_file == 'errors/custom_404.pt'


Attributes


template_file: str

The template to render for the 404 response (the constructor accepts it as four04template_file).

message: Optional[str]

The optional human-readable message describing the error.

title: exceptions.FastAPIChameleonException
text:
Base class for every error raised by fastapi-chameleon.


Usage
Source


exceptions.FastAPIChameleonException()


Raised directly for configuration and rendering problems, such as calling global_init() with a missing or invalid template folder, rendering before global_init() has run, or returning an unsupported type from a decorated view. The control-flow exceptions below subclass it, so catching this type catches them all.
Example:
try:
    fastapi_chameleon.global_init(settings.template_folder)
except FastAPIChameleonException as e:
    raise SystemExit(f'Template folder problem: {e}')

title: Changelog
text:
[0.1.19]

Fixed

global_init() now accepts any os.PathLike (such as pathlib.Path) as the template folder. Previously a Path passed validation but every render then failed inside Chameleon’s loader with TypeError: 'PosixPath' object is not iterable.
The dev optional-dependencies extra is installable on Python 3.10 again: great-docs (which needs 3.11+) now carries a python_version marker.



Documentation

New user guide at https://mkennedy.codes/docs/fastapi-chameleon/user-guide/getting-started.html: Getting Started, Decorating Views, Writing Templates, Friendly Error Pages, Troubleshooting, Testing and CI, Configuration, How It Works, and FAQ. Its pages are included in llms-full.txt.
Replaced the auto-generated Agent Skill with a hand-written skills/fastapi-chameleon/SKILL.md covering the rules of the package (init order, return contract, where not_found() works, TAL not Jinja) rather than only its API names.
Added Example blocks to every public docstring and an entry-point overview to the package docstring.
README links each section to the guide page that expands it, documents Python 3.15 support, and uses Path objects with global_init().
scripts/build_docs.py now fails when llms.txt, llms-full.txt, or the skill files are missing from the built site.
The docs build requires great-docs>=0.17 (pinned in requirements-dev.txt). The 0.13 release that was in the project venv silently drops the package-info page, the lightbox assets, and the Llms-txt lines in robots.txt.
ruff.toml limits Ruff to Python sources and skips docs/ and great-docs/, because Ruff 0.17 formats code blocks inside Markdown by default and would rewrap README and SKILL.md snippets.
tox.ini adds a py315 environment.
Tidied pyproject.toml: removed the dead [tool.setuptools] table and the unused hatch-vcs build requirement, and corrected the sdist excludes (/example_app never existed, so the example app, docs site, and skill were shipping in the sdist).

title: Changelog

[0.1.18]

Added

Ship inline type information to consumers via a py.typed marker (PEP 561), so downstream type checkers can see the package’s annotations.
New dev optional-dependencies extra (pip install fastapi-chameleon[dev]) bundling pytest, ty, and pyrefly.
A full documentation site built with Great Docs (Quarto), published at https://mkennedy.codes/docs/fastapi-chameleon/, including an auto-generated API reference from the package docstrings.
Expanded PyPI keywords for better discoverability (templating, rendering, decorator, ASGI, Starlette, and more).



Changed

Tightened type hints across the public API so the package now passes both ty and pyrefly cleanly: NoReturn on not_found() / generic_error(), typed decorator wrappers and casts, and annotations on global_init(), clear(), and response().
Removed the inaccurate dict element type on **template_data.
Expanded Sphinx-style docstrings for the public API (template, the internal render path, clear) and added :ivar: documentation to the exception types.
Rewrote README.md with a runnable quick start, full public-API reference, friendly-error and view-testing guides, dev-mode/caching notes, a docs badge, and corrected example-app and contributing instructions.

title: fastapi-chameleon
text:
Features

One decorator turns a FastAPI view into a server-rendered HTML page: return a dict, get a rendered template.
Sync and async views are both fully supported.
fastapi.Response pass-through: return a Response (redirect, JSON, etc.) from a decorated view and the template is skipped entirely.
Friendly error pages: not_found() renders a custom 404 page, generic_error() renders any template with any status code.
Template name inference: leave the template name off and it’s derived from the module and function name.
Dev mode: auto_reload=True picks up template edits without restarting the server.
Fully typed: ships inline type hints with a py.typed marker (PEP 561). The decorator uses ParamSpec-based overloads and functools.wraps, so a decorated view keeps its exact parameter signature, so FastAPI’s dependency injection and type checkers like ty and pyrefly keep working.
Tiny dependency footprint: just fastapi and chameleon.

title: fastapi-chameleon
text:
Installation
pip install fastapi-chameleon

title: fastapi-chameleon
fastapi-chameleon
text:
Usage

Project layout
Create a folder within your web app to hold the templates, such as:
├── main.py
├── views.py
│
└── templates
    ├── home
    │   └── index.pt
    ├── errors
    │   └── 404.pt
    └── shared
        └── layout.pt
In the app startup, tell the library about the folder you wish to use:
from pathlib import Path
import fastapi_chameleon

dev_mode = True

BASE_DIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
template_folder = BASE_DIR / 'templates'
fastapi_chameleon.global_init(template_folder, auto_reload=dev_mode)
global_init() accepts a str or any os.PathLike such as pathlib.Path. It validates the folder (it raises FastAPIChameleonException if the path is empty or not an existing directory) and is idempotent by default: a second call is a no-op while templates are already initialized. Pass cache_init=False to force re-initialization (handy in tests).

Order matters: call global_init() before importing/registering your view modules. Template name inference (below) resolves at decoration time; if the engine isn’t initialized yet, the path silently defaults to templates/ relative to the current working directory, which may not be what you want. If you always pass explicit template names, this is much less of a concern.

Every option is listed in the Configuration guide.


Decorating views
Then just decorate the FastAPI view methods (works on sync and async methods):
@router.post('/')
@fastapi_chameleon.template('home/index.pt')
async def home_post(request: Request):
    form = await request.form()
    vm = PersonViewModel(**form)

    return vm.dict()  # {'first': 'Michael', 'last': 'Kennedy', ...}
The view method should return a dict to be passed as variables/values to the template.
If a fastapi.Response is returned, the template is skipped and the response along with status_code and other values is directly passed through. This is common for redirects and error responses not meant for this page template:
@router.post('/account/login')
@fastapi_chameleon.template('account/login.pt')
async def login(request: Request):
    user = await try_login(request)
    if user:
        return fastapi.responses.RedirectResponse('/account', status_code=302)

    return {'error': 'Invalid login'}  # re-render the form with an error
Returning anything other than a dict or a fastapi.Response raises FastAPIChameleonException.
The decorator also accepts a mimetype for non-HTML output, e.g. @fastapi_chameleon.template('seo/sitemap.pt', mimetype='application/xml').


Three ways to use the decorator
@fastapi_chameleon.template('home/index.pt')   # explicit template file
@fastapi_chameleon.template()                  # inferred template name
@fastapi_chameleon.template                    # bare form, also inferred
When no template name is given, it’s derived from where the view lives:

The file is {module}/{function_name} under the template folder, where module is the last segment of the view’s dotted module name.
An .html file is preferred; if it doesn’t exist, .pt is the fallback.
Example: def index() in views/home.py resolves to templates/home/index.html, falling back to templates/home/index.pt.

This resolution happens once at import time, so there is zero per-request filesystem overhead.
A few error behaviors worth knowing:

Calling a decorated view without ever calling global_init() raises FastAPIChameleonException at request time.
Referencing a template file that doesn’t exist raises ValueError (from Chameleon’s loader) when the view is called.

The Decorating Views guide expands on this section, and Troubleshooting lists every error with its fix.

title: fastapi-chameleon
text:
Friendly 404s and errors
A common technique for user-friendly sites is to use a custom HTML page for 404 responses. This is especially important in FastAPI because FastAPI returns a 404 response + JSON by default. This library has support for friendly 404 pages using the fastapi_chameleon.not_found() function.
Here’s an example:
@router.get('/catalog/item/{item_id}')
@fastapi_chameleon.template('catalog/item.pt')
async def item(item_id: int):
    item = service.get_item_by_id(item_id)
    if not item:
        fastapi_chameleon.not_found()

    return item.dict()
This will render a 404 response using the template file templates/errors/404.pt. You can specify another template to use for the response, but it’s not required:
fastapi_chameleon.not_found(four04template_file='errors/custom_404.pt')
not_found() works by raising an exception, so execution stops right there. Code after the call never affects the response. The 404 template is rendered with an empty model.
Because the decorator is what catches the exception, you can call not_found() or generic_error() anywhere beneath a decorated view. Deep in a service or data-access layer works fine. The flip side: calling them from a route that is not decorated with @fastapi_chameleon.template (or from middleware/dependencies) leaves the exception unhandled and FastAPI will return a 500 instead of your error page.
If you need to return errors other than Not Found (status code 404), you can use a more generic function: fastapi_chameleon.generic_error(). It lets you render any error template with any status code:
@router.get('/catalog/item/{item_id}')
@fastapi_chameleon.template('catalog/item.pt')
async def item(item_id: int):
    item = service.get_item_by_id(item_id)
    if not item:
        fastapi_chameleon.generic_error('errors/unauthorized.pt',
                                        fastapi.status.HTTP_401_UNAUTHORIZED)

    return item.dict()
You can also pass data into the error template via the optional template_data dict:
fastapi_chameleon.generic_error('errors/500.pt', 500,
                                template_data={'detail': 'Something went sideways.'})
Note that error pages are always rendered as text/html, regardless of the mimetype passed to the @template decorator. More in the Friendly Error Pages guide.

fastapi-chameleon
text:
API reference
Full, per-function docs are at mkennedy.codes/docs/fastapi-chameleon. The summary below mirrors the public surface.
Everything public is importable straight from fastapi_chameleon:
__all__ = ['template', 'global_init', 'not_found', 'response', 'generic_error']








Function
Signature
Purpose




global_init
global_init(template_folder: str | os.PathLike, auto_reload: bool = False, cache_init: bool = True) -> None
Initialize the template engine once at startup. No-op if already initialized (unless cache_init=False).


template
template(template_file=None, mimetype='text/html')
Decorator for view functions. Usable bare, with empty parens, or with an explicit template path.


response
response(template_file: str, mimetype: str = 'text/html', status_code: int = 200, **template_data) -> fastapi.Response
Render a template and wrap it in a Response with full manual control.


not_found
not_found(four04template_file: str = 'errors/404.pt') -> NoReturn
Abort the view and render a friendly 404 page (always raises).


generic_error
generic_error(template_file: str, status_code: int, template_data: Optional[dict] = None) -> NoReturn
Abort the view and render any error template with any status code (always raises).



Two more functions live in fastapi_chameleon.engine (not exported at package level):








Function
Signature
Purpose




engine.render
render(template_file: str, **template_data) -> str
Render a template directly to an HTML string.


engine.clear
clear() -> None
Reset the cached loader and template path. The test-isolation hook.



Exceptions, in fastapi_chameleon.exceptions:

FastAPIChameleonException(Exception): base class; also raised for bad global_init input, missing init at render time, and invalid view return types.
FastAPIChameleonNotFoundException: raised by not_found(); carries .template_file and .message.
FastAPIChameleonGenericException: raised by generic_error(); carries .template_file, .status_code, .message, and .template_data.

title: fastapi-chameleon
text:
Dev mode, caching, and performance

auto_reload defaults to False: Chameleon caches compiled templates for production performance. Set auto_reload=True during development to pick up template edits without restarting.
Engine state is a single module-global template loader per process. Call global_init() once before serving requests; after that the loader is read-only. See How It Works.

title: fastapi-chameleon
text:
Testing your views
Decorated views remain plain callables, so no TestClient is required. Call them directly (or via asyncio.run() for async views) and inspect the returned fastapi.Response:
# conftest.py
from pathlib import Path

import pytest
import fastapi_chameleon as fc

@pytest.fixture
def test_templates_path(pytestconfig):
    return Path(pytestconfig.rootdir, 'tests', 'templates')

@pytest.fixture
def setup_global_template(test_templates_path):
    fc.global_init(str(test_templates_path))
    yield
    fc.engine.clear()  # don't leak engine state between tests
# test_views.py
# index_view is any view function decorated with @fastapi_chameleon.template(...)
def test_index_renders(setup_global_template):
    resp = index_view()
    assert resp.status_code == 200
    assert 'Hello' in resp.body.decode('utf-8')
This is exactly the pattern this project’s own test suite uses. The Testing and CI guide has async views, TestClient, and a CI matrix.

title: exceptions.FastAPIChameleonGenericException
text:
Signals an arbitrary error response from inside a decorated view.


Usage
Source


exceptions.FastAPIChameleonGenericException(
    template_file, status_code, message=None, template_data=None
)


Raised by generic_error() and caught by the template() decorator, which renders template_file with the chosen status_code. You normally raise it indirectly via generic_error() rather than constructing it yourself.
Example:
try:
    fastapi_chameleon.generic_error('errors/403.pt', 403, template_data={'user': user})
except FastAPIChameleonGenericException as e:
    assert e.status_code == 403 and e.template_data == {'user': user}


Attributes


template_file: str

The template to render for the error response.

status_code: int

The HTTP status code to return.

message: Optional[str]

The optional human-readable message describing the error.

template_data: Optional[dict]

Optional variables passed to the template when rendering.

title: generic_error()
text:
Short-circuit the current view and render an error page with a custom status code.


Usage
Source


generic_error(template_file, status_code, template_data=None)


Like not_found(), but for any error: call it from inside a template()-decorated view to render template_file with the HTTP status_code you choose (for example 401 or 500). The decorator catches the raised exception and builds the response. This function never returns normally.
Example:
if not user.is_admin:
    fastapi_chameleon.generic_error('errors/403.pt', 403, template_data={'user': user})


Parameters


template_file: str

The error template to render (path relative to the template folder).

status_code: int

The HTTP status code to return (for example fastapi.status.HTTP_401_UNAUTHORIZED).

template_data: dict = None

Optional variables passed to the template. Defaults to None (an empty context).





Raises


 FastAPIChameleonGenericException

Always; this is how the error is signalled to the decorator.

title: API Reference
text:
Everything fastapi-chameleon exposes: the template decorator, app setup, error helpers, and the exception types.


Setup

Point the library at your Chameleon templates folder once at app startup.


global_init()

Initialize the Chameleon template engine for your app.




Rendering views

Decorate FastAPI view functions to render templates, or build a response directly.


template()

Decorate a FastAPI view to render its return value through a Chameleon template.

response()

Render a template and return it as a FastAPI response directly.




Error responses

Short-circuit a view to render a friendly error page with the right status code.


not_found()

Short-circuit the current view and render a friendly 404 page.

generic_error()

Short-circuit the current view and render an error page with a custom status code.




Exceptions

Exception types raised by the library (the error helpers raise these internally).


exceptions.FastAPIChameleonException

Base class for every error raised by fastapi-chameleon.

exceptions.FastAPIChameleonNotFoundException

Signals a 404 response from inside a decorated view.

exceptions.FastAPIChameleonGenericException

Signals an arbitrary error response from inside a decorated view.

title: response()
text:
Render a template and return it as a FastAPI response directly.


Usage
Source


response(template_file, mimetype="text/html", status_code=200, **template_data)


Use this when you want a rendered Response without the template() decorator, for example to return a fully-formed response from a view that does its own branching. Requires global_init() to have been called first.
Example:
@app.get('/sitemap.xml')
def sitemap():
    return fastapi_chameleon.response('seo/sitemap.pt', mimetype='application/xml', urls=load_urls())


Parameters


template_file: str

The Chameleon template file to render (path relative to the template folder, *.pt).

mimetype: str = "text/html"

The response media type. Defaults to text/html.

status_code: int = 200

The HTTP status code for the response. Defaults to 200.

template_data={}

Keyword arguments passed through to the template as variables.





Returns


 fastapi.Response

A fastapi.Response containing the rendered template, with the given media type and status code.





Raises


 FastAPIChameleonException

If global_init() has not been called.

# fastapi-chameleon

FastAPI returns JSON by default. fastapi-chameleon renders Chameleon templates instead: call `global_init(template_folder)` once at startup, decorate views with `@fastapi_chameleon.template(...)`, return a `dict`, and the view hands FastAPI a `fastapi.Response` with `text/html`. Package errors are `FastAPIChameleonException` or a subclass. Template errors come from Chameleon as `ValueError`, `NameError`, or `chameleon.exc.*`.

## Install

`uv add fastapi-chameleon` or `pip install fastapi-chameleon`.

## Use

```python
from pathlib import Path
import fastapi
import fastapi_chameleon

app = fastapi.FastAPI()
fastapi_chameleon.global_init(Path(__file__).resolve().parent / 'templates', auto_reload=dev_mode)  # before view modules are imported

@app.get('/')                                   # route decorator outermost
@fastapi_chameleon.template('home/index.pt')    # path relative to the template folder
def index():
    return {'title': 'Home'}                    # dict == template variables; a fastapi.Response is passed through
```

Test form: call the view directly, `resp = index()` or `asyncio.run(index())`, and assert on `resp.status_code` and `resp.body`. Use a fixture that calls `global_init()` and `fastapi_chameleon.engine.clear()` on teardown. CI is `pytest` per interpreter, no extras.

## Rules

- `global_init()` runs once. A second call is ignored unless `cache_init=False` or `engine.clear()` was called first, so you cannot change `auto_reload` by calling it again.
- Call `global_init()` before importing view modules. Bare `@template` infers `{module}/{function}.html` then `.pt` at import time, and if the engine is not initialised yet the folder silently defaults to `templates` under the current working directory and is never re-resolved.
- Views return a `dict` or a `fastapi.Response`. Anything else, including `None` and Pydantic models, raises `FastAPIChameleonException` at request time. Use `model.model_dump()`.
- Returning any `fastapi.Response` skips the template. That is how redirects work from page views.
- `not_found()` and `generic_error()` always raise. They only work below a `@template`-decorated view. From an undecorated route, a dependency, or middleware they become a plain 500; raise `fastapi.HTTPException` there instead.
- `not_found()` renders `errors/404.pt` with an empty model. Only `generic_error()` accepts `template_data`.
- Error pages are always `text/html` at their own status. The decorator's `mimetype` does not apply to them.
- The decorator has no `status_code` parameter. A rendered dict is always 200. Use `response(...)` for other codes.
- Templates are TAL, not Jinja. `${expr}` interpolates and is escaped, `tal:repeat`, `tal:condition`, `tal:content`, `tal:attributes` control flow, `metal:use-macro="load: ../shared/layout.pt"` with `metal:fill-slot` does layouts. There is no `{% %}` or `{ }`.
- `.pt` and `.html` are treated identically by Chameleon. Inference prefers `.html`.
- Dependency injection keeps working on decorated views, sync or async. Path and query parameters, `Request`, and `Depends()` resolve as normal.
- Templates are compiled once per process unless `auto_reload=True`. Keep it off in production.
- `global_init()` accepts `str` or any `os.PathLike`. Versions up to 0.1.18 accepted a `Path` but failed later with `TypeError: 'PosixPath' object is not iterable`; use `str()` there.

## Decision table

| Need | Use |
|---|---|
| Render a template from a sync or async view | `@fastapi_chameleon.template('home/index.pt')` on the view |
| Infer the template from module and function name | bare `@fastapi_chameleon.template` after `global_init()` has run |
| Redirect or return JSON from a page view | return a `fastapi.Response` subclass |
| HTML 404 instead of FastAPI's JSON | `fastapi_chameleon.not_found()` or `not_found('errors/custom.pt')` |
| Any error status with data in the template | `fastapi_chameleon.generic_error('errors/403.pt', 403, template_data={...})` |
| Non-200 status or non-HTML type from a normal view | `fastapi_chameleon.response(template_file, mimetype=..., status_code=..., **model)` |
| Non-HTML type for a decorated view | `@template('seo/sitemap.pt', mimetype='application/xml')` |
| Rendered HTML as a string | `fastapi_chameleon.engine.render(template_file, **model)` |
| Pick up template edits without restart | `global_init(folder, auto_reload=True)` |
| Re-initialise in tests | `global_init(folder, cache_init=False)` or `engine.clear()` |

## API

- `global_init(template_folder: str | os.PathLike, auto_reload: bool = False, cache_init: bool = True) -> None`. Raises `FastAPIChameleonException` for an empty or non-directory path. Idempotent by default.
- `template(template_file: str | None = None, mimetype: str = 'text/html')`. Decorator, usable bare or with arguments. Returns a signature-preserving wrapper.
- `response(template_file: str, mimetype: str = 'text/html', status_code: int = 200, **template_data) -> fastapi.Response`. Manual render. Raises `FastAPIChameleonException` if not initialised.
- `not_found(four04template_file: str = 'errors/404.pt') -> NoReturn`. Raises `FastAPIChameleonNotFoundException`.
- `generic_error(template_file: str, status_code: int, template_data: dict | None = None) -> NoReturn`. Raises `FastAPIChameleonGenericException`.
- `engine.render(template_file: str, **template_data) -> str` and `engine.clear() -> None`. Not in `__all__`; import via `fastapi_chameleon.engine`.
- `exceptions.FastAPIChameleonException` (base), `FastAPIChameleonNotFoundException` (`.template_file`), `FastAPIChameleonGenericException` (`.template_file`, `.status_code`, `.template_data`).

## Reading a failure

```text
fastapi_chameleon.exceptions.FastAPIChameleonException: Invalid return type <class 'NoneType'>, we expected a dict or fastapi.Response as the return value.
    -> the view has no return statement, or returned a model; return a dict
ValueError: Template not found: home/index.pt.
    -> path is relative to the global_init() folder; check folder, subfolder, .pt vs .html, and that global_init() ran before the view module was imported
NameError: items
    -> the template uses a variable the view did not return; add it to the dict or guard with tal:condition
INFO: 127.0.0.1 - "GET /items/9" 500   (log: FastAPIChameleonNotFoundException: The URL resulted in a 404 response.)
    -> not_found() was called outside a @template-decorated view; decorate the route or raise fastapi.HTTPException
```

Fix order: make `global_init()` run once and first with an absolute path, then make the view return a dict, then fix the template path, then read the variable or expression Chameleon names.

## Resources

- Docs: <https://mkennedy.codes/docs/fastapi-chameleon/>
- Getting started: <https://mkennedy.codes/docs/fastapi-chameleon/user-guide/getting-started.html>
- Decorating views: <https://mkennedy.codes/docs/fastapi-chameleon/user-guide/views.html>
- Writing templates: <https://mkennedy.codes/docs/fastapi-chameleon/user-guide/templates.html>
- Error pages: <https://mkennedy.codes/docs/fastapi-chameleon/user-guide/error-pages.html>
- Troubleshooting: <https://mkennedy.codes/docs/fastapi-chameleon/user-guide/troubleshooting.html>
- Testing and CI: <https://mkennedy.codes/docs/fastapi-chameleon/user-guide/testing.html>
- API reference: <https://mkennedy.codes/docs/fastapi-chameleon/reference/>

title: Friendly Error Pages
text:
Somewhere out there is a customer with a bookmark to a Shelf Life book that sold last Tuesday. When they click it, FastAPI’s instinct is to answer {"detail": "Not Found"}. Accurate, and about as welcoming as a locked door with a sticky note on it.
A website should say sorry in HTML. It should keep the header and the search box, suggest a few similar books, and look like the rest of the site. fastapi-chameleon gives you two functions for that: not_found() for the everyday 404, and generic_error() for every other status code you might need.

A friendly 404
@router.get('/catalog/item/{item_id}')
@fastapi_chameleon.template('catalog/item.pt')
async def item(item_id: int):
    item = service.get_item_by_id(item_id)
    if not item:
        fastapi_chameleon.not_found()

    return item.model_dump()
Read that again and notice what is missing. There is no return in front of not_found(), and there is no else. The call does not come back. It renders templates/errors/404.pt with status 404 and the rest of the function never runs.
To use a different template:
fastapi_chameleon.not_found(four04template_file='errors/custom_404.pt')
The 404 template is rendered with an empty model, so it cannot show request-specific data such as the title that was searched for. Keep it static, or reach for generic_error() when the page needs variables.


Any status code with generic_error()
Not every refusal is a 404. A book held for staff review should produce a 403, and the page should be able to say why:
@router.get('/catalog/item/{item_id}')
@fastapi_chameleon.template('catalog/item.pt')
async def item(item_id: int):
    item = service.get_item_by_id(item_id)
    if not item.visible_to(current_user):
        fastapi_chameleon.generic_error('errors/forbidden.pt', fastapi.status.HTTP_403_FORBIDDEN)

    return item.model_dump()
Pass data to the error template with template_data:
fastapi_chameleon.generic_error('errors/500.pt', 500, template_data={'detail': 'Something went sideways.'})


How they work, and where they work
Both functions are emergency exits. They always raise. not_found() raises FastAPIChameleonNotFoundException and generic_error() raises FastAPIChameleonGenericException. The @template decorator, sitting at the top of the call, catches those two exceptions and renders the error template with the right status.
Because the decorator does the catching, the exit can be pulled from anywhere below a decorated view. Shelf Life’s service.get_item_by_id() could call not_found() itself, three layers down from the route, and the customer would still get the page. No status codes threaded back up through return values, no Optional sprinkled across every layer. Execution stops at the call, and the decorator takes it from there.
The flip side follows directly. The exit only works if there is a decorated view above it to catch the exception. Call not_found() from an undecorated route, from middleware, or from a FastAPI dependency and nothing is listening. FastAPI sees an unhandled exception and returns a bare 500 Internal Server Error. In those places, decorate the route or raise fastapi.HTTPException instead.


What the error response looks like









not_found()
generic_error()




Status
always 404
the status_code you pass


Template
errors/404.pt by default, or the one you name
the one you name


Model
empty
template_data, or empty if omitted


Content type
text/html
text/html



The decorator’s mimetype does not apply to error pages. A view decorated with mimetype='application/xml' still delivers its 404 as text/html, because the person reading it is in a browser.
One last thing to set up before the first not_found() call: create templates/errors/404.pt. If the error template itself is missing, Chameleon raises ValueError while trying to render it and the client sees a 500. An error page that errors is a small tragedy, and an avoidable one.


Reference

not_found()
generic_error()
FastAPIChameleonNotFoundException and FastAPIChameleonGenericException

title: Getting Started
Writing Templates
Troubleshooting
text:
It is late, the deploy just went out, and the Shelf Life home page is a white screen with Internal Server Error on it. The server log, happily, knows exactly what happened. This page is the field guide for reading it.
Every error you can meet falls into one of three groups. Errors the package raises itself are FastAPIChameleonException or a subclass, and their messages are written to be read by a human. Errors from Chameleon while compiling or rendering a template arrive as ValueError, NameError, AttributeError, or one of Chameleon’s own types, and they name the file, the variable, or the expression that failed. And then there is behaviour that is working exactly as designed and still looks like a bug until you know the rule. All three groups surface as a 500 in the browser and a traceback in the log, so always start from the log.

title: Troubleshooting
section: FastAPIChameleonException: You must call global_init() before rendering templates.
text:
FastAPIChameleonException: You must call global_init() before rendering templates.
A decorated view, response(), or engine.render() ran before global_init(). The engine has no template folder and nothing to load from. Call global_init(template_folder) once at startup, in the module that creates the app, before requests are served. In tests, use a fixture that calls it and clears the engine afterwards. See Testing and CI.

title: Troubleshooting
section: FastAPIChameleonException: The template_folder must be specified.
text:
FastAPIChameleonException: The template_folder must be specified.
global_init() was called with an empty string or None. Usually a settings value that did not load. Pass the path to your templates folder.

title: Troubleshooting
section: FastAPIChameleonException: The specified template folder must be a folder, it's not: ...
text:
FastAPIChameleonException: The specified template folder must be a folder, it's not: ...
The path does not exist or points at a file. The message shows the path exactly as the package saw it, which is the clue: relative paths resolve against the current working directory, and that directory differs between python main.py, uvicorn main:app, your test runner, and your container. Build the path from __file__ instead and the problem disappears for good:
BASE_DIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
fastapi_chameleon.global_init(BASE_DIR / 'templates')

title: Troubleshooting
section: FastAPIChameleonException: Invalid return type <class 'NoneType'>, we expected a dict or fastapi.Response as the return value.
text:
FastAPIChameleonException: Invalid return type <class 'NoneType'>, we expected a dict or fastapi.Response as the return value.
The view returned something other than a dict or a fastapi.Response. NoneType almost always means a missing return statement. Any other type means a model object, a list, or a string came back from the data layer and was passed straight through. Convert it: model.model_dump() for Pydantic, dataclasses.asdict(obj) for dataclasses, {'items': items} for a list.

title: Troubleshooting
section: 500 Internal Server Error, log shows FastAPIChameleonNotFoundException: The URL resulted in a 404 response.
text:
500 Internal Server Error, log shows FastAPIChameleonNotFoundException: The URL resulted in a 404 response.
not_found() was called from code that is not below a @template-decorated view. The same applies to FastAPIChameleonGenericException: The URL resulted in an error. from generic_error(). The function raised as designed, but nothing above it was listening, so FastAPI treated it as a crash. Decorate the route, or raise fastapi.HTTPException(status_code=404) from undecorated code. See Friendly Error Pages.

title: Troubleshooting
section: TypeError: 'PosixPath' object is not iterable inside chameleon/loader.py
text:
TypeError: 'PosixPath' object is not iterable inside chameleon/loader.py
Versions up to 0.1.18 accepted a pathlib.Path in global_init() without complaint, then handed it to Chameleon’s loader, which tried to iterate it as a list of search paths. Upgrade, or wrap the path in str(). Current versions accept any os.PathLike.

title: Troubleshooting
text:
ValueError: Template not found: home/missing.pt.
The template path does not exist under the folder given to global_init(). The path in the message is relative to that folder, so check for a typo, a wrong subfolder, or .html versus .pt. If the view uses the bare @template form, the expected path is {module}/{function}.html or .pt, where module is the last segment of the view’s module name: a view named index in views/home.py wants home/index.pt. If the path looks right and the file is definitely there, the engine is probably pointing at the wrong folder because global_init() ran after the view module was imported. See Decorating Views.

title: Troubleshooting
text:
NameError: items
The template referenced a variable the view did not return. Chameleon names the missing variable for you. Add it to the dict the view returns, or guard the element with tal:condition. The same error appears when a shared layout uses a variable, such as title, that one of its pages forgot to provide.

title: Troubleshooting
text:
AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'upper'
An expression inside ${ } or a tal: attribute failed partway through. Chameleon appends the expression that failed, for example - Expression: "title.upper()", so you know exactly which line of the template to look at. Fix the data the view returns, or make the expression tolerate the value.

title: Troubleshooting
text:
chameleon.exc.LanguageError or chameleon.exc.ExpressionError
The template itself has a bug: an invalid tal: attribute such as tal:repeat="x" without a sequence to repeat over, or a Python expression with a syntax error. These are raised the first time the template is compiled, which is the first request that uses it, so a template nobody has visited since the last edit can carry a broken expression into production unnoticed. The message includes the offending string and the file name.

title: Troubleshooting
section: Template edits are not showing up
text:
Template edits are not showing up
You edited the template, refreshed, and nothing changed. Templates are compiled once and cached. Pass auto_reload=True to global_init() during development. If you already did and it still happens, check whether global_init() is being called twice: the second call is ignored unless cache_init=False, so the first call’s settings win. See Configuration.

title: Troubleshooting
section: The wrong template renders, or the bare @template form cannot find a file that exists
text:
The wrong template renders, or the bare @template form cannot find a file that exists
Template name inference runs when the view module is imported, using whatever folder is configured at that moment. If global_init() had not run yet, the folder defaulted to templates relative to the current working directory, and a later global_init() did not go back and re-resolve the name. Move global_init() above the view imports, or name the template explicitly.

title: Troubleshooting
text:
My 404 page returns JSON
The request never reached a decorated view. No route matched, so FastAPI’s router answered on its own, in JSON. Add a catch-all route decorated with @template that calls not_found(), or register a FastAPI exception handler for 404 that returns fastapi_chameleon.response('errors/404.pt', status_code=404).

title: Troubleshooting
section: The error page itself fails with a 500
text:
The error page itself fails with a 500
The error template is missing or broken. not_found() renders errors/404.pt by default, so create that file. A ValueError: Template not found: errors/404.pt. in the log confirms this cause.
